Risk: Administrator identity or credential store compromised
Threat event: An attacker gains the administrator's AWS credentials and second factor through phishing, a compromised identity account or a stolen unlocked device, and takes control of the AWS account, including the ability to delete data and backups
Existing controls (verified): MFA on AWS root and admin user; MFA on administrator identity accounts; no AWS access keys on the operator's computer (CloudShell only); budget alerts
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Low: MFA blocks password-only attacks, but the factors are not independent, so one compromise can yield both. Impact Very High: full control of production and backups
Planned action: Move AWS root and admin MFA to phishing-resistant factors (security keys or passkeys) kept outside the password store; lock backups against deletion (AWS Backup Vault Lock); test admin recovery (with R-19)

Risk: Malicious deploy through a compromised identity or code-host account
Threat event: An attacker takes over the identity account that signs in to the code host, pushes a change to main, and the pipeline deploys an app that captures users' passphrases
Existing controls (verified): MFA on the code host and identity account; deploy role usable only from the main branch of one repository; 1-hour deploy sessions; full Git history of every change
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Low: MFA on both accounts, but no approval step stands between a push and production. Impact Very High: every user's data readable from then on (breaks SC-1)
Planned action: Phishing-resistant MFA (passkey or security key) on the identity account and code host; give the code host its own sign-in; email notification on every production deploy; review the code host security log monthly

Risk: Unreviewed change breaks the app or corrupts data
Threat event: The operator pushes a faulty change (for example a sync or encryption bug) that deploys straight to production and breaks the app or damages stored records
Existing controls (verified): CI runs unit tests and a type check before every deploy; deploys only from main; rollback by revert; DynamoDB deletion protection and point-in-time recovery; encrypted copies on users' devices
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Moderate: frequent solo changes with no second review. Impact Moderate: point-in-time recovery and device copies limit lasting loss
Planned action: Work on branches with a pull request and a self-review checklist; CI runs on pull requests before merge; each merged PR is the change approval record

Threat event: The operator, deliberately or under pressure, deploys app code that captures users' passphrases
Existing controls (verified): Git history makes any code change visible after the fact; users know the operator personally
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Very Low: no motive and personal relationships with every user. Impact Very High: all content readable
Planned action: Accepted at design time: the risk cannot reach zero while the operator serves the code, even with a second person. Add a free detective control: a changelog of every production deploy that users can see. Re-assess if a second admin is added (T-06) or users who are not friends or family join (T-04)

Risk: Malicious dependency or Action runs in the deploy job
Threat event: A compromised npm package or GitHub Action runs inside the deploy job, uses the deploy credentials, and changes the app or the AWS account
Existing controls (verified): Small direct dependency set (2 runtime, 5 development packages); no long-lived AWS keys in CI (OIDC); 1-hour sessions; deploy role limited to main; CI tests
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Low: supply-chain attacks are common but untargeted, and the direct dependency set is small; the transitive tree is much larger. Impact Very High: the deploy role is administrator-equivalent
Planned action: Commit a lockfile and install with npm ci; give the deploy credentials only to the deploy step; pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs; turn on Dependabot alerts; later, narrow the CDK deploy permissions

Risk: Incident goes undetected or cannot be investigated
Threat event: An attack or misuse in the AWS account or app is not noticed, or cannot be reconstructed afterwards because the needed logs do not exist
Existing controls (verified): Budget alerts; AWS CloudTrail event history (AWS default, 90 days, management events); Lambda error logs (14 days)
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Moderate: no security alerting at all today. Impact High: affected users could not be told what was exposed
Planned action: Free controls only (no GuardDuty, a cost decision): verify or create a CloudTrail trail with log file validation; free email alerts on root and admin sign-in and on logging changes; keep app logs longer. Remaining Moderate risk to be accepted with a written reason after treatment

Threat event: An attacker or someone close to a user gets their password and authenticator code (phishing, reuse, access to their phone) and signs in as them
Existing controls (verified): Invite-only accounts; TOTP MFA required; 10-character minimum password; generic sign-in errors; 1-hour tokens; API throttling; end-to-end encryption means a taken-over account exposes only ciphertext
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Low: MFA required and a small, invite-only user base. Impact Moderate: the attacker gets ciphertext only but could delete that user's records (recoverable)
Planned action: Move the user pool to the Cognito Essentials plan (free under 10,000 monthly users) and offer passkey sign-in, which resists phishing; tell users how to protect their account in the Phase 6 privacy notice

Threat event: Someone who already holds a user's keyring (for example after an AWS breach) guesses a weak passphrase offline and decrypts that user's data
Existing controls (verified): PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations; passphrase at least 12 characters; 24-character random recovery code; keyring reachable only after another compromise (R-01, R-02, R-05)
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Very Low: needs a prior AWS compromise plus a weak passphrase. Impact High: one user's content
Planned action: Add a self-hosted passphrase strength check (block common passphrases, encourage several words), with no third-party scripts

Risk: Record metadata shows when users log
Threat event: The operator, AWS or anyone who reaches the table sees record names and timestamps that show which days each user logged something
Existing controls (verified): Only record names, timestamps and sizes are visible, never content; table access limited to the operator
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Moderate: the operator sees metadata whenever doing support. Impact Moderate: activity dates of several users
Planned action: Change how records are named so stored keys no longer reveal dates (for example, keys derived with the user's data key); only sync timestamps would remain. Engineering change in the app

Risk: Deleted users remain in backups for years
Threat event: A user leaves and asks for deletion, but encrypted copies of their data stay in backups for up to 3 years
Existing controls (verified): Backups hold ciphertext only, unreadable without the user's passphrase
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Moderate: someone among 10 users may leave in a given year. Impact Low: data is unreadable; harm is to trust and promises
Planned action: Retention schedule and plain disclosure in the privacy notice (Phase 6); decide whether 3-year copy retention is needed

Threat event: A user or a person they record complains, or a law applies, and there is no notice, terms or record of how requests were handled
Existing controls (verified): Users are known personally; content is end-to-end encrypted; commitments made in the invitation email and setup screens
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Low: friends and family are unlikely to complain formally. Impact High: formal complaint or consumer health law exposure (trigger T-03)
Planned action: Privacy notice and terms, a request log, and the applicable-law analysis including non-user data (Phase 6)

Threat event: A bug, an admin mistake (such as deleting the wrong account) or an AWS fault destroys records, and the restore fails or was never practised
Existing controls (verified): Point-in-time recovery (35 days); daily backups (35 days) with a cross-region copy (3 years); table deletion protection; encrypted copies on users' devices
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Low: several independent copies exist, but restore has never been recorded as tested. Impact High: a user's history lost for good
Planned action: Run and record a restore test at least yearly; bring the copy vault into infrastructure code or document it; backup lock (with R-01)

Risk: Operator unavailable for an extended period
Threat event: The operator cannot run the service for weeks (illness, life events); nobody else can fix problems, help users or keep the account paid
Existing controls (verified): Serverless service runs without intervention; domain auto-renews; backups are automatic; users keep encrypted copies on their devices
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Low. Impact High: an outage of more than a week is possible and users have no way to export their data
Planned action: A short continuity note for a trusted person (what to tell users, how to shut down cleanly); turn the user backup download back on

Threat event: An AWS fault, a traffic flood or abuse of the API makes sync unavailable or runs up the bill
Existing controls (verified): App works offline and syncs later; API throttling (10 requests/second, burst 20); CloudFront in front of all traffic; AWS Shield Standard (provided by AWS); budget alerts
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Moderate: regional AWS issues happen. Impact Low: the app keeps working offline
Planned action: Accept; within the moderate appetite for outages

Risk: Domain or DNS hijacked, or domain lapses
Threat event: The domain is transferred, its DNS changed or it expires, and users are sent to a fake app that captures passphrases
Existing controls (verified): Registration and DNS protected by AWS account controls (R-01); auto-renew on; HSTS for one year; TLS certificate validated by DNS
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Very Low: needs an AWS compromise or a registrar failure. Impact Very High: a fake app could capture passphrases
Planned action: Free checks under the confidentiality rule (methodology 4.2): verify registrar transfer lock, auto-renew, contacts and renewal payment, and add them to the Phase 4 automated checks. Residual risk cannot reach zero; the aim is verified controls with evidence

Risk: User mailbox exposes invitation password or recovery code
Threat event: Someone with access to a user's mailbox uses the temporary password or a self-emailed recovery code
Existing controls (verified): Temporary password expires in 7 days and must be changed; TOTP still required to sign in; a recovery code alone cannot sign in
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Low. Impact Low: the attacker still needs the user's authenticator to reach any data
Planned action: User guidance on storing the recovery code in the Phase 6 privacy notice

Threat event: A flaw such as cross-site scripting lets an attacker run script in the app and read decrypted data in the browser
Existing controls (verified): Strict Content Security Policy (scripts only from the app's own origin, no inline scripts); no third-party scripts or frameworks; framing blocked; no referrer sent
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Very Low: strict CSP and no third-party code. Impact Very High: plaintext readable in the browser
Planned action: Add Trusted Types to the Content Security Policy (require-trusted-types-for 'script'), free under the confidentiality rule; keep the CSP strict and re-assess if any third-party script or framework is added

Threat event: A flaw in the sync API lets one user read, change or delete another user's records
Existing controls (verified): JWT required on every API route; Lambda takes the user ID only from the verified token; user ID and record key bound into each ciphertext; API unit tests
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Very Low: the user ID never comes from the request body. Impact Moderate: content stays encrypted; records could be altered or deleted
Planned action: Add cross-user tests for the two API routes not yet covered (single-record read and delete), so every route is checked on every deploy

Threat event: The operator loses their phone and cannot get back into AWS or the code host because recovery has never been tested
Existing controls (verified): Account recovery options on the identity accounts; AWS root account recovery process (provided by AWS)
Scoring rationale: Likelihood Low. Impact High: no fixes or account changes possible for more than a week
Planned action: Test recovery of administrator access from a new device; keep printed break-glass recovery codes stored offline
